title: Aristotle Companion File: Role and Three Targets
content: Lines 1-16 explain this file's role: it is an Aristotle companion exposing routine supporting lemmas for the automated proof-search tool. The three targets are listed explicitly: (1) upperExponent_increasing — geometric sequence monotonicity; (2) oddNumbers_card — counting odd numbers in {1,...,2N}; (3) oddNumbers_no_triple — parity pigeonhole. This design separates provable supporting infrastructure from the main open problem and axiomatized results.
mathContext: Aristotle companion files follow the pattern: `import Mathlib`, one namespace, definitions shared with the main file, then theorem stubs. Each theorem has a `/- PROBLEM ... PROVIDED SOLUTION ... -/` block explaining the expected proof strategy. Lines 17-22 set up the environment: single `import Mathlib`, `open Finset Real`, `namespace Erdos866`.

title: Four Core Definitions: Interval, HasAllPairwiseSums, oddNumbers, upperExponent
content: Four definitions establish the mathematical objects. `Interval N` = `(Finset.range (2*N+1)).filter (· ≥ 1)` gives {1,...,2N}. `HasAllPairwiseSums A b` = `∀ i j : Fin k, i < j → (b i + b j).toNat ∈ A` uses witnesses `b : Fin k → ℤ`. `oddNumbers N` = `(Interval N).filter (· % 2 = 1)`. `upperExponent k : ℝ` = `1 - (2 : ℝ)⁻¹ ^ k` (noncomputable).
mathContext: The integer witness type `Fin k → ℤ` (rather than `Fin k → ℕ`) allows negative witnesses. The `.toNat` coercion handles out-of-range sums: negative integers map to 0, which is outside `Interval N` (filtered to ≥ 1), so the condition `(b i + b j).toNat ∈ A` fails automatically. The `noncomputable` annotation on `upperExponent` reflects that ℝ in Lean uses classical axioms. The `oddNumbers` definition composes two filters: first {1,...,2N} via `Interval`, then odd elements.

title: upperExponent_increasing: One-Line Proof of Geometric Monotonicity
content: Theorem: `upperExponent k < upperExponent (k+1)` for k ≥ 1. The Aristotle docstring (lines 40-47) suggests the proof strategy: unfold `upperExponent`, use `sub_lt_sub_iff_left` to reduce to `(2⁻¹)^(k+1) < (2⁻¹)^k`, then apply `pow_lt_pow_right` with base in (0,1). The actual proof (line 50) achieves this in a single compound `exact`: `sub_lt_sub_left (pow_lt_pow_right_of_lt_one₀ (...) (...) (...)) _`.
mathContext: The chain: `upperExponent k < upperExponent (k+1)` unfolds to `1-(2⁻¹)^k < 1-(2⁻¹)^{k+1}`, which by `sub_lt_sub_left h _` requires `(2⁻¹)^{k+1} < (2⁻¹)^k`. Since $0 < 2^{-1} < 1$ (proved by `norm_num`) and $k+1 > k$ (from `hk : k ≥ 1` via `linarith`), `pow_lt_pow_right_of_lt_one₀` closes the goal. The subscript `₀` indicates the version for strict positivity. No `ring_nf` normalization is needed since the statement already has the right form.

title: oddNumbers_card: Bijection Proof of |{1,3,...,2N-1}| = N
content: Theorem: `(oddNumbers N).card = N`. Proved via `Finset.card_eq_of_bijective` with explicit bijection `fun i hi => 2*i+1` from `{i : ℕ | i < N}` (encoded as `Fin N` via the bijective API). The proof has three obligations: (1) surjectivity: each odd n gives witness `n/2` with membership proved by `linarith` and `Nat.mod_add_div`; (2) injectivity: `grind` via arithmetic; (3) image membership: `aesop`.
mathContext: The bijection $i \mapsto 2i+1$ maps $\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}$ bijectively to $\{1,3,\ldots,2N-1\}$. For surjectivity: given odd $n \in \text{oddNumbers}(N)$, the witness is $n/2$ (floor division). The key identity `Nat.mod_add_div n 2` gives `n = n%2 + 2*(n/2)`, so since `n%2 = 1`, we get `n = 2*(n/2)+1`. The range conditions `1 ≤ n` and `n ≤ 2N` then force `0 ≤ n/2 < N`. The `linarith` calls chain these constraints together from the membership hypotheses extracted by `Finset.mem_filter.mp`.

title: oddNumbers_no_triple: Parity Contradiction via simp_all and grind
content: Theorem: `¬∃ b : Fin 3 → ℤ, HasAllPairwiseSums (oddNumbers N) b`. The proof has three steps. First, `rintro ⟨b, hb⟩` destructs the assumption. Second, `h_odd` is derived: for all `i < j : Fin 3`, `(b i + b j).toNat % 2 = 1` — the membership in `oddNumbers` forces parity 1. The `aesop` in `h_odd` handles the filter membership unfolding. Third, `simp_all +decide [Fin.forall_fin_succ]` expands the ∀ over `Fin 3` and `grind +ring` closes the arithmetic contradiction.
mathContext: The parity arithmetic: if $b_0+b_1 \equiv 1$, $b_0+b_2 \equiv 1$, $b_1+b_2 \equiv 1$ (all mod 2), then adding the first two and subtracting the third: $(b_0+b_1)+(b_0+b_2)-(b_1+b_2) = 2b_0 \equiv 1+1-1 = 1$ (mod 2). But $2b_0 \equiv 0$ (mod 2) — contradiction. Lean's `grind +ring` can discover this via ring normalization combined with modular arithmetic. The `Fin.forall_fin_succ` lemma unfolds `∀ i : Fin (n+1), P i` as `P 0 ∧ ∀ i : Fin n, P i.succ`, reducing the three-way ∀ to three explicit cases that `decide` can handle.
